📺 WHY PROS BUY OPTIONS INSTEAD OF SHARES BEFORE EARNINGS $MSFT & $META EXAMPLES

$MSFT and $META delivered two completely different earnings outcomes, but together they illustrate one of the most important lessons in trading: professionals don't judge a trade solely by whether it made money—they judge whether the risk was managed correctly.

*

$MSFT trade was a textbook example of using defined-risk options.

A $410/$420 bull call spread offered an attractive setup, risking about $2 to potentially make $8.

After earnings, #Microsoft rallied above $425, allowing traders who followed the plan to capture most or all of the maximum profit. It was a high-probability trade with a favorable risk-to-reward profile.

*

$META told a very different story.

I bought 10 Meta $690 call options for roughly $10 each, risking about $10,000 on the earnings event.

The stock moved against me, and those options fell dramatically in value. Some traders suggested averaging down, but I refused.

The broader market wasn't supporting aggressive risk-taking, and there was no reason to increase exposure simply because the options had become cheaper.

*

The bigger mistake came from traders who ignored risk management altogether.

Instead of buying options, they purchased large stock positions ahead of earnings simply because they believed Meta would report strong results.

When Meta sold off after earnings, the consequences were dramatically different.

A trader holding around 1,000 shares near $630 would have lost roughly $100,000 after a 100-point decline.

By comparison, the options trade I took lost only the premium paid. The loss was planned, limited, and fully understood before entering the position.

*

That is the key advantage of options for almost all earnings trades. They provide defined risk. No matter how wrong the trade becomes, your maximum loss is predetermined.

Traders shouldn't take oversized stock positions into binary events like earnings. Predicting earnings is difficult, even when you like the company. What matters is ensuring one bad trade cannot seriously damage your account.

So, the goal isn't to win every trade. The goal is to stay in the game long enough to participate in the next high-probability opportunity.

*

$MSFT demonstrated how disciplined options strategies can generate exceptional returns when the trade works. $META demonstrated something even more valuable: losing the right way is just as important as winning.

Successful trading isn't about avoiding losses—it's about controlling them. That's the difference between professionals who survive for decades and traders who eventually blow up their accounts.
